analysis.text:
Gamini Perera was allotted Lot A depicted in Partition Plan No. 2525 dated 2 February 1981, made by S. Silva, Licensed Surveyor, bearing Assessment No. 20, Flower Road, Homagama, containing in extent 10 perches, by a final decree of a partition case bearing No. 111/P dated 2 February 1985 entered in the District Court of Homagama.

Gamini Perera, by Deed of Gift No. 515 dated 10 March 1986, attested by R. Liyanage, Notary Public, gifted the said Lot A depicted in Plan No. 2525 absolutely and irrevocably to his son, Suresh Perera, subject to the life interest of Gamini Perera and his wife Vinitha. Gamini Perera died on 12 June 1990 due to heart failure. Vinitha revoked her life interest over the said Lot A depicted in Plan No. 2525 by Deed of Revocation of Life Interest No. 525 dated 25 February 1991, attested by S. Sapumal, Notary Public.

Suresh Perera married Kanthi and had two children, namely Rakitha and Muditha. Muditha died due to an accident on 5 June 2023, unmarried and issueless. Rakitha married Ann and died on 2 July 2022.

Suresh Perera died on 10 December 1995 intestate. Suresh Perera had an offspring named Samantha from his first marriage, who is a citizen of the United States of America.

1. Draw up the pedigree showing the devolution of title from Gamini Perera up to the present owners in relation to the land and premises bearing Assessment No. 20, Flower Road, Homagama. **(15 marks)**
2. What are the shares presently owned by each heir in the property? **(4 marks)**
3. Can Samantha become entitled to the intestate estate of Suresh Perera? Discuss with reference to the provisions of the Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act No. 38 of 2014, as amended by the Land (Restrictions on Alienation) (Amendment) Act No. 21 of 2018. **(2 marks)**
4. Explain the rules set out in sections 22 to 26 of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance No. 15 of 1876. **(4 marks)**

**Total: 25 marks**

claims.text: Yes, Samantha can become entitled to the intestate estate of Suresh Perera. Under Section 2(1)(a) of the Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act No. 38 of 2014, the transfer of title of land to a foreigner is generally prohibited. However, Section 3(1)(d) provides an express exemption for any land the title of which is transferred by intestacy, gift, or testamentary disposition to a next of kin who is a foreigner, in accordance with the applicable law of succession of Sri Lanka.

Under Section 22 of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance No. 15 of 1876, when a person dies intestate leaving a surviving spouse, the surviving spouse inherits one-half of the property of such person. This inheritance does not relieve a husband from any legal liability to maintain his children. The rules in sections 23 to 26 cannot be explained as they are omitted from the provided text.

answer.question:
Gamini Perera was allotted Lot A depicted in Partition Plan No. 2525 dated 2 February 1981, made by S. Silva, Licensed Surveyor, bearing Assessment No. 20, Flower Road, Homagama, containing in extent 10 perches, by a final decree of a partition case bearing No. 111/P dated 2 February 1985 entered in the District Court of Homagama.

Gamini Perera, by Deed of Gift No. 515 dated 10 March 1986, attested by R. Liyanage, Notary Public, gifted the said Lot A depicted in Plan No. 2525 absolutely and irrevocably to his son, Suresh Perera, subject to the life interest of Gamini Perera and his wife Vinitha. Gamini Perera died on 12 June 1990 due to heart failure. Vinitha revoked her life interest over the said Lot A depicted in Plan No. 2525 by Deed of Revocation of Life Interest No. 525 dated 25 February 1991, attested by S. Sapumal, Notary Public.

Suresh Perera married Kanthi and had two children, namely Rakitha and Muditha. Muditha died due to an accident on 5 June 2023, unmarried and issueless. Rakitha married Ann and died on 2 July 2022.

Suresh Perera died on 10 December 1995 intestate. Suresh Perera had an offspring named Samantha from his first marriage, who is a citizen of the United States of America.

1. Draw up the pedigree showing the devolution of title from Gamini Perera up to the present owners in relation to the land and premises bearing Assessment No. 20, Flower Road, Homagama. **(15 marks)**
2. What are the shares presently owned by each heir in the property? **(4 marks)**
3. Can Samantha become entitled to the intestate estate of Suresh Perera? Discuss with reference to the provisions of the Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act No. 38 of 2014, as amended by the Land (Restrictions on Alienation) (Amendment) Act No. 21 of 2018. **(2 marks)**
4. Explain the rules set out in sections 22 to 26 of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance No. 15 of 1876. **(4 marks)**

**Total: 25 marks**

claims.text: Under the Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act, No. 12 of 2006, the stamp duty for a transfer or conveyance of immovable property (other than by gift) where the value exceeds Rs. 100,000 is Rs. 3.00 for every Rs. 100 of the value not exceeding Rs. 100,000, and Rs. 4.00 for every Rs. 100 or part thereof of the value exceeding Rs. 100,000. For a land value of Rs. 100,000,000, the duty is Rs. 3,000 for the first Rs. 100,000 and Rs. 3,996,000 for the remaining Rs. 99,900,000, yielding a total stamp duty of Rs. 3,999,000.

According to the Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) (Amendment) Act, No. 10 of 2008, stamp duty is paid by affixing adhesive stamps to the required value prior to, or at the time of, the execution of the instrument, and the value must be specified on its face. Furthermore, under the Stamp Duty Act, No. 43 of 1982, the stamp duty on a conveyance is payable by the grantee (the purchaser) unless there is an agreement to the contrary.

claims.text: Under the Notaries Ordinance, a notary is generally required to search the registry to ascertain the state of the title of the land and check if prior deeds have been registered, but this search is not compulsory if the parties to the transaction authorize the notary in writing to dispense with it.
If authorized in writing to dispense with the search, the notary must write the reference at the head of the instrument before it is tendered for registration.
None of the supplied statutory provisions contain the procedure or rules to be followed when a notary has an interest (personal or familial) in the transaction.

No, this is not permitted. Under the proviso in the Notaries Ordinance, a title search is only non-compulsory if the parties to the transaction authorize the notary in writing to dispense with the search. A request by an employer does not satisfy this statutory requirement.

> **Note:** This page was blurred. The wording below is reconstructed from the visible text.

A Notary who has practised in Homagama since approximately 1987 intends to apply for appointment/registration under the Registration of Title Act No. 21 of 1998 and other relevant written law.

1. How do the requirements under the relevant law apply to the Commissioner of Title Settlement and to what types of land would title be registered? **(4 marks)**
2. Could both the owner and occupier make an application in respect of the land? Can the application be rejected without an inquiry? **(4 marks)**
3. A deed affecting land is executed, but the instrument is not presented for registration within the prescribed period. Is registration mandatory, and what is the legal consequence of non-registration? **(4 marks)**
4. Who may present an instrument for registration according to the Registration of Title Act/Registration of Documents Ordinance? **(3 marks)**

**Total: 15 marks**

claims.text: Under the Registration of Title Act No. 21 of 1998, 'land' is defined to include land covered with water, any benefit arising out of any land, and all things attached to the earth or permanently fastened thereto.
Under the same Act, 'registered land' is defined as a land parcel (an area of land separately delineated on the cadastral map) the title to which is registered under the Act.

Under Section 7(1) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance, an unregistered instrument is void as against all parties claiming an adverse interest thereto on valuable consideration by virtue of any subsequent instrument which is duly registered.
Registration under the Registration of Documents Ordinance does not cure any defect in the instrument or confer upon it any effect or validity except for the priority conferred under that section.

Under Section 40(1) of the Registration of Title Act No. 21 of 1998, an instrument for conveying interest in a land parcel may be presented for title registration to the Registrar of Title by: (a) any person claiming any interest or benefit thereunder; (b) any person having any interest in or charge on any land affected thereby; or (c) any person attesting such instrument.

limitations: The retrieved sections of the Registration of Title Act No. 21 of 1998 and the Registration of Documents Ordinance do not contain the complete statutory provisions regarding the Commissioner of Title Settlement's procedural requirements, nor do they detail the full rules on application procedures and their rejection.

Part 4: omitted an unsupported draft claim (The claim is directly supported by Section 40(2) of the Registration of Title Act No. 21 of 1998, but it does not answer the question 'Who may present' (as it specifies the method of presentation, i.e., through post or under cover).).

Part 4: omitted an unsupported draft claim (The cited provisions (Sections 13 and 28 of the Registration of Documents Ordinance) do not state who is authorized to present an instrument for registration. Section 13(7) merely refers to a notary who prepared the instrument or the person presenting it in the context of reference details, and Section 28(1) refers to returning the registered instrument to the person who presented it or their agent. Neither section defines who is legally permitted to present it.).

claims.text: The Registrar may refuse to register an instrument if he suspects the presenter is not authorized (until right of presentation is proved) or if the instrument does not comply with the Ordinance or written laws regarding form or mode of execution. The Registrar must refuse registration if the instrument is liable to stamp duty but not duly stamped, if the registration fee is unpaid, or if an instrument (other than a will) does not state the mandatory land description particulars required by section 13.

If an error or omission is shown to the satisfaction of the Registrar-General, he shall issue a written notice in the prescribed form to the parties (for a deed), the executor/administrator (for a will), or the presenter (for other instruments). He then orders the correction, which is made by the concerned Registrar in the prescribed manner without affecting prior accrued priority. If the required notice cannot be issued due to death, legal incapacity, or other sufficient cause, the Registrar-General may still make the correction order upon proof by an interested person. If the error and correction are in different folios, they must be connected by cross-references. An aggrieved person may challenge a refusal by instituting a suit in the District Court within thirty days.
